paras: The lynching of Alvin McKanna was the burning to death of a man accused of murder, robbery and arson by a crowd of local men in Bigby Fork, northern Monroe County, Mississippi, on December 18 or 19, 1880. McKanna, who had given the name Miller, was accused of helping to rob and kill William Brown Ridings, his wife and their young daughter and burning their house over them. Wire reports carried the story across the country as a crime of exceptional horror met with fitting retribution, and it drew editorial argument between Northern and Southern papers.

Ridings was a young man raised in the neighborhood who had married and built a cottage near his parents, about twenty miles from Tupelo. According to a letter to the Aberdeen Examiner, McKanna had spent a week or more in the area posing as a laborer, had worked briefly for a Mr. Lee, and had been refused lodging at the Ridings house a week earlier.

Tupelo dispatches said two men giving the name Miller asked to stay the night on Saturday, December 18, and were given a bed in the family's only room with a fireplace; the Aberdeen letter dated the visit to Friday, December 17, and named only McKanna as the lodger. Around eleven o'clock neighbors saw the cottage burning, and the charred remains of the family were found in the ruins. Missing money and a silver watch raised suspicion, and footprints leading into the woods were judged to be McKanna's.

Parties of men set out in pursuit, and the wire said one suspect was found hidden in a field six miles from Aberdeen, while the Aberdeen letter placed the capture in an untenanted house on the William B. Hogan place, twelve miles from the scene. He was taken back to the scene, where he reportedly confessed to chloroforming and robbing the family and setting the fire, and according to the Aberdeen letter he led his captors to the stolen goods. The Memphis wire said a crowd of twenty-five 'resolute men' pinioned him, arranged pine splinters around him and set him on fire, while New Orleans Times and Picayune specials gave seventy-five men and said he was fastened to a stake or a tree. The Aberdeen Examiner and the Terre Haute Gazette reported that he was hanged as well as burned.

In the confession reported by a Tupelo Journal writer, the man gave his name as Alvin McKanna, aged thirty, of Ashland County, Ohio, an escaped life convict, and named his accomplice as John Gillmore. The Aberdeen letter added that Gilmore had killed Ridings and his wife with an axe, and the Terre Haute Gazette identified McKanna as 'Piney', convicted in Vigo County, Indiana, of the murder of a Dr. Armstrong. Search for the second man was reported as continuing, but the coverage does not report his capture, and no inquest or action against the crowd appears in it.

The Memphis wire, printed in Wheeling, Richmond, New York, Knoxville and elsewhere, said the crowd 'determined the devil should be punished with his own weapon,' under headlines such as 'Fearful Retribution' and 'an avenging crowd.' Mississippi papers ran the Tupelo specials under the heading 'Judge Lynch', and an Okolona paper had predicted before the news of the burning that 'Judge Lynch would try him.' Shorter items in Northern and Western papers, some with garbled names such as 'Mettler' and 'Tripalo', reported the burning without comment, and a December 29 Indiana news summary placed it at 'Mr. Rideing's house in Tupelo.'

The Aberdeen correspondent turned the case into a warning against 'birds of prey' from 'Northern sinks of crime' and called for stricter vagrancy enforcement against tramps. When the Norristown (Pa.) Herald cited the burning as evidence of Mississippi barbarism, the Delaware State Journal answered by pointing to a lynching near Bethlehem, Pennsylvania. The Terre Haute Gazette, reprinted in Jackson's Weekly Clarion, blamed the Indiana jury that had spared him and praised Mississippi, where 'it has not gone out of fashion to kill those who shed blood.' No report gives the race of McKanna, the Ridings family or the crowd.

The Tupelo dispatches dated the murder to Saturday night and the lynching to the following night, while the Aberdeen letter, written December 21 with fuller local detail, dated the murder to Friday, December 17, and the capture to Saturday. Accounts also differ on the size of the crowd, the place of capture, and whether the family was burned after being chloroformed or first killed with an axe, the last point resting entirely on the captured man's reported confession.

reader.title: Lynching of Alvin McKanna
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd of local men, after a citizens' pursuit, put a captured murder suspect to death by burning (and, in local and Indiana accounts, hanging) at the scene of the crime (A1, A7, A22, A23).

Independent Memphis, Picayune, New Orleans Times and Aberdeen Examiner accounts agree that one of the accused men was caught, taken back to the scene and burned by a crowd, though they differ on dates and details (A1, A7, A13, A20, A22).

accounts.label: Memphis wire (Tupelo special)
accounts.gist: Two men named Miller lodged with Brown Riding's family, chloroformed and robbed them and set the cottage on fire; one was found hidden in a field six miles from Aberdeen, confessed at the scene, and 25 resolute men pinioned him with pine splinters and set him on fire.

accounts.label: Picayune and N.O. Times specials (Tupelo, Dec. 20)
accounts.gist: The man was caught near Evergreen (Picayune) or in a pea vine pen near Aberdeen (Times), returned to the scene and burned at a stake or tree by seventy-five resolute men; the Times writer got the confession 'from one present'.

accounts.label: Aberdeen Examiner letter ('Citizen', Dec. 21)
accounts.gist: McKanna lodged with the Ridings family on Friday, Dec. 17, chloroformed them and whistled for Gilmore, who killed the couple with an axe; McKanna was tracked, caught on the Hogan place twelve miles away, led his captors to the stolen goods, and according to the Examiner was hung and burned by the citizens.

accounts.label: Terre Haute (Ind.) Gazette
accounts.gist: Identified the man as 'Piney', convicted in the Dr. Armstrong murder, and said his captors forced a confession, hanged him and burned his body.

framing.detail: The Memphis wire carried to Wheeling, Richmond and New York said the crowd 'determined the devil should be punished with his own weapon'; headlines ran 'Fearful Retribution' and 'an avenging crowd'.
Mississippi papers ran the specials under 'Judge Lynch' and blamed Northern 'tramps' and lax vagrancy enforcement rather than the crowd.
The Terre Haute Gazette, reprinted in Jackson, praised Mississippi where 'it has not gone out of fashion to kill those who shed blood' and attacked the Indiana jury that spared him.
The Delaware State Journal called it 'a horrible crime was horribly punished' and, citing a Pennsylvania lynching, rejected the Norristown Herald's charge of Mississippi barbarism.
Northern and Western papers ran short summaries of the burning without comment.
